title: Identification and Authentication Failures

levels.beginner: Login is the front door. Authentication failures happen when the door can be opened without the right key: weak passwords allowed, no limit on guesses, sessions that never expire, or password-reset links that can be guessed.
levels.intermediate: Common patterns: credential stuffing against logins with no rate limiting, weak password policies, session tokens that are predictable or never invalidated after logout or password change, and multi-factor authentication missing on privileged accounts.
levels.advanced: Defend in layers: strong, breached-password-checked credentials; rate limiting and lockout with care for denial-of-service; random, expiring, revocable session tokens stored hashed server-side; MFA for admin and sensitive actions; and a password-reset flow whose tokens are random, single-use and short-lived.

key_points: Allow long passphrases; check new passwords against known breach lists.
Rate-limit login attempts per account and per IP; log failures.
Session tokens must be random, expire, and be revocable on logout and password change.
Require MFA for privileged accounts and sensitive actions.
Password-reset tokens: random, single-use, short-lived, sent only to the registered address.

defensive_examples.title: Store only a strong hash, never the password
defensive_examples.code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()
stored = ph.hash(plain_password)   # store `stored`, never the password
ph.verify(stored, plain_password)  # raises on mismatch
defensive_examples.explanation: Argon2id is a memory-hard hash designed for passwords. If the database leaks, attackers still face a slow, expensive guess for every password.

defensive_examples.title: Session cookie flags (defensive configuration)
defensive_examples.code: Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=604800
defensive_examples.explanation: HttpOnly keeps scripts from reading the token, Secure sends it only over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax limits cross-site sending.

knowledge_check.question: An attacker tries thousands of passwords against one account and the app never slows them down. Which weakness is this?
options: Missing rate limiting / improper restriction of authentication attempts
knowledge_check.explanation: Unlimited guesses make brute force and credential stuffing practical. Rate limiting and lockout are the standard countermeasures.

knowledge_check.question: After a user changes their password, what should happen to their other active sessions?
options: They should be revoked, forcing re-login
They should be made admin sessions
They should be shared with the user by email
knowledge_check.explanation: A password change usually means the account may be compromised, so other sessions must be invalidated.
